title: One parcel fee, many item charges
hook: A fixed parcel fee is different from a fee attached to each item.
question: A fictional parcel costs €3 plus €0.50 per item. Items can share one parcel or each use a parcel. For four items, which charge is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional policy; shared parcel permitted; no other fees.
details: A fictional parcel costs €3 plus €0.50 per item. Items can share one parcel or each use a parcel.
principle: The per-item charge repeats either way, but the fixed parcel fee repeats only with separate parcels. Labeling a cost as fixed requires naming the thing it is fixed per.

title: Average the quantities too
hook: Mixing different quantities makes a simple average of unit prices misleading.
question: Material A costs €3/kg and B €6/kg. Compare 1kg of each with 2kg A plus 1kg B. Which mixture has the lower average price at A=2kg?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional prices; additive masses; no mixing guidance.
details: Material A costs €3/kg and B €6/kg. Compare 1kg of each with 2kg A plus 1kg B.
principle: Total price divided by total mass weights each unit price by its quantity. The simple mean of €3 and €6 only describes equal masses. A larger share of the cheaper material shifts the weighted mean downward.
objective: Compute a quantity-weighted average rather than averaging unit prices blindly.
misconception: A mixture’s average unit price is always the simple mean of its labels.

title: Capacity changes batch count
hook: Twenty objects and a six-object carrier: a remainder still needs another trip.
question: Ideal carriers hold exactly six or eight identical objects. Objects cannot be split; capacity is assumed usable. For twenty objects, which needs fewer batches?

details: Ideal carriers hold exactly six or eight identical objects. Objects cannot be split; capacity is assumed usable.
principle: Divide object count by usable capacity and round up. The partial final batch still counts as a complete trip in this quantity-only model. Volume, weight and safe carrying limits would require separate constraints.

title: Move the decimal with the unit
hook: 125 cents is not €12.50. The unit tells you the conversion factor.
question: A euro contains 100 cents. A divides cents by 100; B deliberately divides by ten instead. For 125 cents, which conversion is correct?
assumptions: Scaled model; unit arithmetic; 100 cents/€; B deliberately wrong.
details: A euro contains 100 cents. A divides cents by 100; B deliberately divides by ten instead.
principle: The denominator comes from the unit definition: one hundred cents per euro. Dividing by ten changes the amount by the wrong factor. Carry the unit alongside the digits so the decimal movement has a reason.
objective: Convert cents to euros using the stated unit relationship.
misconception: Converting cents to euros requires moving the decimal only one place.

title: Round lines or round the total
hook: Rounding three tiny lines separately can differ from rounding their sum once.
question: Each fictional line is exactly €0.335 before rounding. A rounds each line to cents; B sums first and rounds once. For three lines, which modeled result is higher?
assumptions: Scaled model; toy rule: nearest cent, half upward; no billing-law claim.
details: Each fictional line is exactly €0.335 before rounding. A rounds each line to cents; B sums first and rounds once.
principle: Rounding loses information at each application. Three rounded €0.34 lines sum to €1.02, while €1.005 rounded once gives €1.01 under the stated half-up rule. Actual billing conventions need their own rule.
objective: Compare line-level rounding with aggregate rounding under a stated convention.
misconception: Rounding before summing is always identical to rounding after summing.
